red-fox-meadow.hint: Foxes come back once smaller animals are here. They need cover for a den and a healthy meadow.
red-fox-meadow.diet: Voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds, and bugs. Also berries
red-fox-meadow.preferredHabitat: Meadows, farm edges, and hedges across open land
red-fox-meadow.fact: When hunting mice, red foxes tend to pounce facing northeast. They seem to use the Earth like a compass to judge the jump.
red-fox-meadow.role: A clever mid-sized hunter that keeps mice and rabbits in check. It stalks low, then pounces. It also eats bugs, berries, and dead animals. No bigger hunters live here, so the fox sits near the top.

lady-beetle.hint: Flowers bring aphids. Aphids bring lady beetles.
lady-beetle.diet: Hunts aphids and other small, soft bugs
lady-beetle.shelter: Winters in leaf litter in big groups. Rests on leaves
lady-beetle.fact: One lady beetle can eat about 5,000 aphids in its life. That is about 50 a day.
lady-beetle.role: A small hunter that eats aphids and other soft bugs, both when young and when grown. That makes it a great helper in gardens. Birds and bigger bugs then eat it, which links the aphids up the food web.

western-meadowlark.hint: Meadowlarks need wide native grass to nest. They also need water to drink and bathe.
western-meadowlark.diet: Mostly bugs in summer. Seeds and grain in winter
western-meadowlark.role: A grassland bird that eats lots of grasshoppers, crickets, and beetles in summer. In winter it eats seeds. All that eating keeps bug numbers down. It is round and feeds on the ground, so hawks and other meadow hunters catch it.

red-tailed-hawk.hint: Hawks look for a meadow that is already full of small animals.
red-tailed-hawk.diet: Mostly small mammals like voles, squirrels, and rabbits. Also birds and snakes
red-tailed-hawk.preferredHabitat: Open land: grassland, fields, and meadows seen from above
red-tailed-hawk.fact: That sharp eagle cry in movies is almost always a red-tailed hawk.
red-tailed-hawk.role: The top day hunter of the meadow. It rides the wind on wide wings or watches from a perch. By eating voles, ground squirrels, rabbits, and birds it keeps plant eaters in check. Almost nothing hunts a grown hawk here.

barn-owl.hint: A quiet, healthy meadow with lots of voles and a dark place to rest.
barn-owl.diet: Almost all small mammals: voles, mice, and shrews, hunted at night
barn-owl.shelter: Nests in tree holes, cliff cracks, and quiet buildings
barn-owl.fact: A barn owl’s heart-shaped face guides sound so well it can catch prey in the dark by ear alone.
barn-owl.role: The night hunter of mice. It flies low and silent over the grass and swallows mice whole, which keeps mouse numbers down. Nothing here hunts it.

woodpecker.hint: Woodpeckers need dead standing trees. Leave some up.
woodpecker.diet: Mostly bugs: beetle grubs, ants, and caterpillars. Some berries and sap
woodpecker.shelter: Holes it cuts itself in dead standing trees. Sleeps in them all year
woodpecker.preferredHabitat: Open leafy and mixed woods with dead trees full of bugs
woodpecker.fact: The downy woodpecker is small. It can dig into weed galls for fly grubs. Bigger woodpeckers cannot reach them.
woodpecker.role: Woodpeckers eat the beetles and bugs that live in wood and bark, which takes pressure off the trees. The holes they leave behind become homes for nuthatches, wrens, and flying squirrels. Hawks, owls, squirrels, and snakes hunt them.

great-horned-owl.hint: Tall trees, quiet shelter, and prey animals that are already back.
great-horned-owl.diet: Mammals and birds: rabbits, voles, squirrels, skunks. Also frogs
great-horned-owl.preferredHabitat: Old woods broken up by open ground, in almost every area
great-horned-owl.fact: Great horned owls are one of the few hunters that kill and eat skunks. The spray does not seem to bother them.
great-horned-owl.role: This owl sits at the top of the forest at night. It eats a wider range of prey than any other owl or hawk in North America. It holds down rabbits, squirrels, chipmunks, and even other owls, so those numbers jump when it is gone. Nothing hunts the adults, only the eggs and chicks.

black-bear.hint: Bears only come back to a rich forest. They need berries, water, shelter, and space.
black-bear.shelter: Dens in hollow trees, roots, rock cracks, or dug holes. Sleeps all winter
black-bear.preferredHabitat: Thick forest with dense brush and lots of berries and nuts
black-bear.fact: Black bear cubs are born in winter sleep and weigh under half a pound. That is the smallest newborn compared to adult size of any furry animal.
black-bear.role: Black bears eat almost anything. They spread berry seeds, dig up bugs, and now and then take deer and elk babies. They are the most common big meat eater in North American forests. They tie the nut, bug, and animal layers together. Nothing hunts a grown bear.

elk-forest.hint: Grassy clearings and water in a healthy forest.
elk-forest.shelter: No den. Calves hide in thick plants. The herd watches out together
elk-forest.preferredHabitat: Grassy clearings and open wood edges inside a bigger forest
elk-forest.fact: In Yellowstone, elk are about 85% of what wolves eat in winter. Their leftovers feed at least a dozen other animals.
elk-forest.role: Elk are big grazers. Heavy grazing shapes grass, willow, and aspen, and those plants come back when elk numbers drop. They are the main food of wolves, big cats, and bears, so they hold the big hunters up, and when one dies many scavengers eat. Their yearly moves spread goodness up and down the mountain.

bobcat.hint: Bobcats follow lots of prey. They need rocks and brush to hide in.
bobcat.diet: Eats only meat: rabbits, mice, and squirrels. Some birds and lizards
bobcat.preferredHabitat: Forest with thick brush, scrub, and rocky ground
bobcat.fact: In the eastern US, bobcat numbers rise and fall with how many rabbits there are.
bobcat.role: Bobcats are key mid-sized hunters. They hold down rabbits, mice, and squirrels, which eases the pressure on forest plants. They sit below cougars and wolves and above the small animals they take. They shape whole groups of small animals.

garter-snake-forest.hint: A sunny rock pile next to grassy hunting ground.
garter-snake-forest.diet: Worms, frogs, and slugs. Also leeches, fish, and small mice
garter-snake-forest.shelter: Shared winter dens in burrows and rock piles. Hides under logs
garter-snake-forest.fact: Garter snakes are the main hunter of the poison rough-skinned newt. Some have grown able to survive its poison.
garter-snake-forest.role: Garter snakes are all-purpose hunters that hold down worms, slugs, frogs, and small fish. In the Northwest they are the main check on rough-skinned newts, and they can handle the newt poison that kills other animals. That makes them famous to scientists. Hawks, crows, and bigger hunters eat them.

beaver.hint: Water channels you have fixed, mud banks, and woody plants.
beaver.diet: Bark and soft wood from willow and aspen, plus water plants
beaver.fact: Beaver dams make wetlands that hold water and support hundreds of other kinds of life.
beaver.role: The builder of the wetland. By cutting trees and damming streams, beavers make new ponds, raise the water, and build the home that most marsh animals need.

freshwater-fish.hint: Clean pools joined together with reeds bring fish back. Then everyone who eats fish follows.
freshwater-fish.fact: Minnow schools are the base that herons, otters, and mink all depend on.
freshwater-fish.role: The base of the wetland food web. These small schooling fish eat algae, plankton, and bug babies. Then almost every marsh hunter eats them.

burrowing-owl.hint: Burrows that are already dug, and open ground to hunt over.
burrowing-owl.fact: It makes a rasping call like a rattlesnake to scare visitors out of its burrow.
burrowing-owl.role: A small owl that lives in holes other animals dug. It hunts bugs by day and mice by night, so it holds down both. Badgers, coyotes, and snakes hunt it.

ptarmigan.hint: Alpine shrubs and quiet cover to nest in, with frostflowers in bloom.
ptarmigan.preferredHabitat: High open ground above the trees all year. Winters in willow hollows
ptarmigan.fact: It is the only bird in North America that lives above the tree line all year.
ptarmigan.role: A mountain bird that hides so well you can walk right past it. It eats buds, leaves, and seeds, and lives almost only on willow in winter. Each winter it grows feathered snowshoes on its feet. Eagles, foxes, weasels, and martens hunt it and its chicks.

golden-eagle.hint: Eagles come last. They arrive when the high country is truly alive again.
golden-eagle.diet: Marmots, hares, ground squirrels, and birds. Also dead animals
golden-eagle.preferredHabitat: Open high country with cliffs and plenty of mid-sized prey
golden-eagle.fact: Golden eagles sometimes line the nest with leaves that smell sweet. It may keep bugs away.
golden-eagle.role: The top hunter of the high country. It drops from the sky on marmots, hares, ptarmigan, and even small meat eaters. It only shows up when the mountain is full of prey. Almost nothing hunts a grown eagle.

sea-otter.hint: Kelp and shellfish beds come first. Otters follow.
sea-otter.diet: Sea urchins, crabs, mussels, clams, and other shellfish
sea-otter.preferredHabitat: Kelp forest and rocky shore with lots of shellfish
sea-otter.role: A key animal of the coast. By eating sea urchins it stops them from mowing down the kelp. So kelp forests and everything living in them can thrive. It also eats a lot of mussels and clams along the rocks.

dolphin.hint: A clean, busy shore brings dolphins in close.
dolphin.fact: Bottlenose dolphins call each other by name. Each one has its own whistle.
dolphin.role: A smart hunter that works with others to herd fish and chase squid near shore. Big sharks and orcas can hunt it. But here it is a top hunter, and seeing one means the coast is full of fish.

migrating-whale.hint: Only a truly healthy shore brings a whale. Watch the horizon.
migrating-whale.diet: Tiny shrimp-like animals, strained out of the sea floor mud
migrating-whale.fact: Gray whales travel up to 14,000 miles there and back. That is one of the longest trips of any mammal.
migrating-whale.role: A whale that feeds on the sea floor. It rolls on its side, sucks up mud, and strains out tiny shrimp-like animals. Killer whales are its main danger. A whale passing by means the coast is fully healed.

northern-leopard-frog.hint: A lily pool and a few open water tiles.
northern-leopard-frog.fact: Leopard frogs escape with wild zig-zag leaps straight back into the water.
northern-leopard-frog.role: A wide-mouthed frog. It eats almost any small animal it can swallow, even other frogs. Herons, mink, and snakes need it for food.

boreal-toad.hint: A snowmelt pool and a few open water tiles.
boreal-toad.diet: Beetles, ants, flies, and other small crawlers. Tadpoles eat algae
boreal-toad.preferredHabitat: High wet meadows with open pools to breed in
boreal-toad.fact: Rocky Mountain boreal toads have crashed because of a deadly skin fungus.
boreal-toad.role: The only toad of the high country. It eats bugs, breeds in shallow snowmelt pools, and takes years to grow up. Its tadpoles eat algae. A skin fungus has wiped out many southern groups, so people work hard to save it.

green-heron.hint: Plant a water tupelo next to a lily pool and open water.
green-heron.diet: Mostly small fish. Also bugs, crabs, and frogs
green-heron.shelter: Stick nests in trees and shrubs that hang over water
green-heron.fact: The green heron drops bait on the water to pull fish close enough to grab.
green-heron.role: A small, clever heron of shady shallows. It is one of the few birds that uses tools. It fishes with great patience. Sometimes it drops bait on the water to pull fish in close.

elf-owl.hint: Plant a mesquite and an ironwood next to a cactus patch.
elf-owl.fact: The world’s smallest owl pulls the stinger off scorpions before eating them.
elf-owl.role: The smallest owl in the world. It hunts bugs and scorpions at night and nests in old woodpecker holes. Snakes and bigger owls are a danger to it.

mountain-chickadee.hint: Plant a subalpine fir and a bent pine with mountain flowers.
mountain-chickadee.diet: Bugs and spiders in summer. Pine seeds and nuts in fall and winter
mountain-chickadee.shelter: Old woodpecker holes and tree holes in pines and aspens
mountain-chickadee.role: A busy little bird that picks bugs off pine twigs and lives on seeds it hid away in winter. Mixed flocks often form around it, and it spreads pine seeds. Small hawks, weasels, and martens eat it and its chicks.

killdeer.hint: Open native grass with a rock pile and a stone wall to nest by.
killdeer.fact: Killdeer fake a broken wing, dragging it as if hurt to lead hunters away from the nest.
killdeer.role: A bug eater that runs and stops, runs and stops across open ground. It grabs worms and bugs as it goes. It nests right out on the ground where it can be seen. So meadow hunters take the adults, the chicks, and the eggs.

red-admiral.hint: Flowers for butterflies and wild flowers, next to a bug hotel.
red-admiral.diet: Adults like tree sap, old fruit, and nectar. Young eat nettles
red-admiral.shelter: Young fold nettle leaves into little tents. Adults rest on trees
red-admiral.preferredHabitat: Flowery clearings and wood edges near nettle patches
red-admiral.fact: Red admirals are bold and defend their patch. They will land on people who stay still.
red-admiral.role: A fast butterfly that guards its own patch. It feeds mostly on tree sap, fruit, and droppings, and drinks from flowers when nothing better is around. Its caterpillars eat only stinging nettle. It has no bad taste to protect it, so it hides and flies fast to get away.

chuckwalla.hint: A rock crack to squeeze into, cactus and brush to eat, and a warm stone pile to sit on.
chuckwalla.fact: A scared chuckwalla wedges into a crack and puffs up its lungs to lock itself in.
chuckwalla.role: A big plant-eating lizard that feeds on desert leaves, flowers, and fruit among the boulders. Hawks, kestrels, coyotes, and rattlesnakes hunt it. When scared it puffs up with air so it gets stuck tight in a rock crack.

alpine-chipmunk.hint: A pile of loose rock and a rock pile among mountain flowers.
alpine-chipmunk.preferredHabitat: High rock slopes and rocky meadows of the Sierra Nevada
alpine-chipmunk.fact: It lives higher than almost any other chipmunk, up to 3,900 meters.
alpine-chipmunk.role: A tiny high-mountain seed eater. It buries seeds and helps spread mountain plants across the rocks. It also takes eggs from rosy-finch and sparrow nests. Foxes, weasels, martens, and hawks all hunt it.

cascades-frog.hint: A snowmelt pool next to a talus pile, with open water close by.
cascades-frog.diet: Eats bugs and spiders in and near the water
cascades-frog.shelter: Snowmelt ponds and lakes. Sleeps the winter in soil under the lake bed
cascades-frog.preferredHabitat: Cold high ponds and streams near pine forest
cascades-frog.fact: It stays active in near-freezing snowmelt water. It suns itself on wet rocks.
cascades-frog.role: A mountain frog built for the cold. It eats bugs and spiders, and its tadpoles eat algae in snowmelt pools. It links pond life to bigger hunters. Trout brought in by people eat its tadpoles, and its numbers have dropped sharply in the south.

black-turnstone.hint: Tidepools and kelp wrack with a driftwood pile to hide in.
black-turnstone.fact: Turnstones flip over stones and shells to grab the creatures hiding beneath.
black-turnstone.role: A shore bird that pries barnacles and limpets loose. It also flips seaweed to find food hidden under it. It helps hold down shore bug numbers, and it needs rich rocky shores.

pigeon-guillemot.hint: A nesting cliff above open water, near an oyster bed.
pigeon-guillemot.fact: This seabird has bright red feet and a bright red mouth.
pigeon-guillemot.role: A seabird that dives and chases small fish. It also pulls small animals out of cracks near the sea floor. It nests in rocky cliffs. It needs the healthy fish and shelter that kelp forests give.

bat-star.hint: A couple of tidepools with an eelgrass bed.
bat-star.role: A sea star that eats almost anything. It pushes its stomach out over the sea floor to break down algae and dead animals. It is the cleanup crew of the shallows. It keeps tidepools and eelgrass beds tidy.

cottontail-rabbit.preferredHabitat: Meadows and field edges with bushes to dash into
cottontail-rabbit.fact: Cottontails rest in shallow dips in the ground called forms. They do not dig burrows.
cottontail-rabbit.role: A grass eater that most meadow hunters depend on. It feeds on grass, clover, and twigs, and it has many babies to make up for how many are eaten. Foxes, hawks, owls, and badgers all live on rabbits.

monarch-butterfly.diet: Young ones eat only milkweed. Adults drink flower nectar
monarch-butterfly.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and roadsides with milkweed and flowers
monarch-butterfly.fact: Monarchs travel up to 3,000 miles. No one butterfly makes the whole trip. It takes a few lifetimes.
monarch-butterfly.role: This butterfly lays eggs only on milkweed. Milkweed is poisonous. The poison stays in the caterpillar and in the grown butterfly. Bright orange wings warn birds to keep away, so almost nothing eats it. Adults feed on late flowers and move pollen.

song-sparrow.diet: Bugs in summer. Seeds and fruit all year
song-sparrow.fact: A male song sparrow can learn about 20 tunes and sing hundreds of versions of them.
song-sparrow.role: A small ground bird that eats bugs while nesting and seeds and fruit the rest of the year. So it keeps bugs down and spreads seeds. There are lots of them, so meadow hawks and snakes eat them often. They link the tiny life on the ground to the big hunters.

mule-deer.shelter: Sleeps in bushes, tall grass, or forest edges. No den
mule-deer.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and shrubland with food and water close by
mule-deer.fact: Mule deer are named for their big, mule-like ears. Each ear turns on its own to find where a sound came from.
mule-deer.role: A big plant eater that shapes the meadow by eating shrubs and leaves. Its eating and its droppings feed the soil and keep plants in check. The animals that would hunt it do not live in this meadow, so little bothers it here.

ground-squirrel.diet: Mostly seeds, grass, and flowers, plus bugs like grasshoppers
ground-squirrel.shelter: Big burrows with many doors, dug in open ground
ground-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Open grassy meadows and slopes near rocks to watch from
ground-squirrel.fact: Facing a rattlesnake, these squirrels kick sand and wave hot tails. The heat jams the snake’s way of seeing.
ground-squirrel.role: A digging animal that eats seeds, greens, and bugs. Its holes let air into the soil, and old holes become homes for others. Hawks, foxes, snakes, and badgers all hunt it. Its towns hold the meadow food web together.

garter-snake-meadow.diet: Worms, frogs, slugs, small fish, bugs, and small mice
garter-snake-meadow.shelter: Hides under rocks and logs. Winters in shared dens
garter-snake-meadow.fact: Garter snakes have a mild venom for their tiny prey. They are harmless to people.
garter-snake-meadow.role: A common meadow hunter that eats worms, frogs, fish, bugs, and small mice. Its spit is a little poisonous, just enough to slow small prey. It keeps bugs and frogs in check. Hawks, owls, and foxes eat it.

bumblebee.diet: Nectar for energy and pollen for growing, from many flowers
bumblebee.shelter: Nests in old mouse burrows, grass clumps, or holes in the ground
bumblebee.fact: Bumblebees shake their flight muscles to knock pollen loose. Tomatoes and blueberries need this to make fruit.
bumblebee.role: A big, fuzzy bee that visits many kinds of flowers for nectar and pollen. It buzzes to shake pollen loose, which most bees cannot do. That makes it key to meadow plants. Spiders and birds hunt it.

grasshopper.diet: Eats plants: grasses, sedges, and broad-leaved weeds
grasshopper.fact: Grasshoppers hear through eardrums on their belly, not their head.
grasshopper.role: The main plant eater of the meadow and the main food too. It turns grass into food for many hunters. Birds, snakes, mammals, and other bugs all eat it. When grasshoppers boom, the whole food web feels it.

barn-swallow.preferredHabitat: Open land near water, flowers, and buildings
barn-swallow.fact: Barn swallows build cup nests from up to 1,000 beakfuls of mud.
barn-swallow.role: A bird that catches flying bugs in the air. It follows cows and tractors to grab the bugs they stir up. It keeps flies and other pests in check. Fast hawks hunt both the grown birds and the young.

tree-squirrel.diet: Acorns, nuts, seeds, tree buds, and fungi. Sometimes bugs and eggs
tree-squirrel.shelter: Dens in tree holes and leaf nests built high up
tree-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Old leafy or mixed forest full of oaks and hickories
tree-squirrel.fact: Gray squirrels bury thousands of nuts each year. The ones they forget grow into new trees.
tree-squirrel.role: Squirrels eat a lot of seeds. But they also bury nuts and forget them, and those nuts grow into new trees. They spread helpful fungus too, and now and then they raid bird nests. There are so many of them that almost every forest hunter eats them.

forest-salamander.diet: Small crawlers: mites, springtails, spiders, beetles, ants, and worms
forest-salamander.shelter: Under logs, rocks, and damp leaves. Hides in soil holes
forest-salamander.preferredHabitat: Cool, damp forest floor with lots of fallen wood
forest-salamander.fact: In some woods, all these tiny salamanders together weigh more than all the birds.
forest-salamander.role: This little salamander rules the leaf litter. It eats the tiny mites and springtails that break down dead leaves. There are so many of them that snakes, birds, and small mammals count on them for food. It breathes through its skin, so it shows whether the forest is damp and healthy.

red-fox-forest.diet: Mice, rabbits, birds, and lizards. Also bugs and fruit
red-fox-forest.shelter: Dens dug into slopes, or taken from other animals. Used for years
red-fox-forest.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and mixed scrub. Avoids thick unbroken forest
red-fox-forest.fact: Red foxes have about 28 different calls. Other foxes can tell each one apart by voice.
red-fox-forest.role: The red fox is a handy mid-sized hunter that keeps mice, rabbits, and ground-nesting birds in check. The fruit it eats spreads seeds. It sits below bears and bobcats and above the small animals it hunts. Fox pairs often use and add on to the same den for years.

mule-deer-forest.diet: Eats leaves, twigs, and weeds in summer. Acorns and berries in winter
mule-deer-forest.shelter: No den. Sleeps in thick shrubs and forest cover to stay warm and safe
mule-deer-forest.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and open woods with shrubs to eat and water
mule-deer-forest.fact: A bounding mule deer gives off an alarm smell from its back legs. Every deer nearby knows at once.
mule-deer-forest.role: Mule deer are big plant eaters that shape which shrubs and young trees grow back. They are key food for big hunters, and their fawns feed bobcats, foxes, and bears. The way they move with the seasons carries goodness across the land.

raccoon.diet: Eats what it finds: crayfish, bugs, frogs, fish, small mammals, eggs, and fruit
raccoon.shelter: Likes hollow tree dens. Also rock cracks, burrows, and buildings
raccoon.preferredHabitat: Damp forest near water for finding food
raccoon.fact: A raccoon’s paws have about four times more touch sensors than its eyes have light sensors.
raccoon.role: Raccoons eat almost anything. They hold down crayfish, frogs, and bugs, spread fruit seeds, and raid bird nests. There are lots of them, so they tie the water and the forest together. Coyotes, big owls, and bobcats keep their numbers down.

porcupine.diet: Eats only plants. Inner bark in winter. Buds, twigs, and leaves in summer
porcupine.shelter: Rock dens, hollow logs, and treetops. Uses the same dens each season
porcupine.preferredHabitat: Pine and mixed forest with trees whose bark it can eat
porcupine.fact: The fisher is one of the few hunters that can kill a porcupine. It flips it over to reach the soft belly.
porcupine.role: Porcupines strip bark, which kills or bends trees. That makes dead trees for hole-nesting birds and gives the forest more shapes. They eat nuts, so they share that food with deer and squirrels. Fishers hunt them most, and bobcats and bears eat them now and then.

chipmunk.shelter: Burrows up to 10 m long with rooms for sleeping and food
chipmunk.preferredHabitat: Old leafy forest with logs, stumps, and rocks to hide in
chipmunk.fact: Chipmunks do not really sleep all winter. They wake up to eat from food stores bigger than a bottle of milk.
chipmunk.role: Chipmunks bury seeds in many small spots. So they spread tree seeds and helpful fungus and help the forest grow back. They eat lots of bugs in summer. There are many of them, so everything from weasels to owls eats them. Their holes let air into the soil and shelter other small animals.

nuthatch.diet: Bugs and spiders in summer. Seeds, acorns, and stored nuts in winter
nuthatch.shelter: Tree holes and old woodpecker holes in big trees. Also nest boxes
nuthatch.preferredHabitat: Old leafy and mixed forest with big oaks and hickories
nuthatch.fact: Nuthatches wipe smelly bugs around their nest hole. It may hide their smell from squirrels.
nuthatch.role: Nuthatches eat the bugs that live in bark, like tent caterpillars and wood borers, which helps hold pests down. They wedge acorns and seeds into bark, which moves seeds a short way. They tie the bug layer to the seed layer, and hawks and owls eat them.

banana-slug.diet: Dead leaves, fungus, rot, and droppings. Sometimes young plants
banana-slug.shelter: Under logs and bark. Seals itself in slime when it gets dry
banana-slug.fact: Seeds and fungus spores pass through a banana slug alive. It plants them as it crawls.
banana-slug.role: Banana slugs break down dead leaves and droppings and put the goodness back in the soil. They spread seeds and fungus, so they help both plants and the fungus web that feeds the trees. Their slime numbs mouths, so few animals eat them. Mostly garter snakes and shrews do.

great-blue-heron.diet: Fish, frogs, and small water animals. Also voles and other birds
great-blue-heron.role: The tall, patient watcher of the shallows and the top hunter of the wetland fish. It steps slowly, then strikes faster than you can see.

wetland-salamander.diet: Worms, bugs, small crawlers, and even small animals with backbones
wetland-salamander.fact: The tiger salamander is one of the biggest on land in North America.
wetland-salamander.role: A hungry digger that hunts worms and bugs near its breeding pools. Its young grow in pools with no fish, and they will even eat each other.

dragonfly.diet: Flying bugs as an adult. Young ones in the water eat mosquito young and tadpoles
dragonfly.shelter: Reed stems above water. The young live in the water
dragonfly.role: A top bug hunter both in the air and under water. Adults grab flying bugs. The young live in the water and eat mosquito babies and tiny fish.

damselfly.diet: Small flying bugs as an adult. Young ones eat small water animals
damselfly.fact: Damselflies fold their wings together over the back when resting. Dragonflies do not.
damselfly.role: A slim flier that scoops midges and mosquitoes out of the air with its legs. Its young live in water, hunt tiny bugs, and feed marsh fish and frogs.

water-strider.diet: Bugs caught on the water surface. Also eats dead ones
water-strider.fact: Water striders ride on top of the water. Their legs are covered in thousands of tiny hairs.
water-strider.role: A bug that skates on top of the water. It grabs insects caught in the surface and cleans up dead ones. Fish, frogs, and wading birds catch it easily.

desert-cottontail.diet: Grasses, mesquite, cactus pads, and other desert plants
desert-cottontail.role: A common desert plant eater that feeds on grass and twigs. Foxes, coyotes, bobcats, and hawks all live on it. Its numbers help hold up the desert hunters.

mountain-goat.shelter: Shallow beds scraped into cliff ledges and rocky ground
mountain-goat.preferredHabitat: Steep high cliffs with escape routes above the grass
mountain-goat.role: A sure-footed climber that grazes the highest cliffs. It eats grass, small plants, and lichen off the rock. Its rubbery hooves grip ground that few hunters can follow. Cougars still take young and grown goats, and eagles snatch newborns off ledges.

bighorn-sheep.preferredHabitat: Open grassy mountain slopes next to rough, rocky cliffs
bighorn-sheep.fact: Bighorns escape across rock ledges only a few inches wide.
bighorn-sheep.role: A grazer of open, steep slopes. It crops grass and small plants and stays close to cliffs it can escape into. Rams crash their horns together each fall with a boom you can hear far off. Cougars hunt lambs and adults, and eagles may take the very young.

pika.diet: Grass, weeds, and wildflowers, gathered and dried into hay piles for winter
pika.preferredHabitat: Rock slopes and stone piles next to high flower meadows
pika.fact: Pikas cut and dry little haystacks of plants to eat under the winter snow.
pika.role: A tiny cousin of rabbits that lives in rock piles. It drives the whole mountain food web. All summer it cuts and dries little haystacks of plants so it can eat under the snow. Weasels, martens, foxes, and eagles all hunt it.

marmot.preferredHabitat: Open meadow patches with boulders and ground to burrow in
marmot.fact: About 98 out of every 100 marmots that die in summer are caught by a hunter.
marmot.role: A round rodent that loves to sun itself. It grazes meadow plants and fattens on seeds before sleeping eight months. Groups whistle from boulder lookouts to warn each other. Golden eagles, coyotes, and foxes hunt them.

snowshoe-hare.diet: Green plants in summer. Buds, twigs, bark, and pine needles in winter
snowshoe-hare.shelter: Shallow hollows under thick shrubs and pine cover
snowshoe-hare.preferredHabitat: Brushy thickets and thick undergrowth near open grass
snowshoe-hare.role: A hare of brushy cover near treeline. Its coat flips from brown to white with the seasons. Its numbers rise and fall about every ten years, and hunter numbers rise and fall with them. Martens, foxes, eagles, and owls all hunt it.

elk-alpine.preferredHabitat: High summer meadows near tree cover and snowmelt water
elk-alpine.role: A big grazer that moves with the seasons. It spends summer in high meadows, walking uphill after fresh grass, and calls all through the fall. Bulls grow huge new antlers every year. Cougars take grown elk, and eagles and coyotes may take newborn calves.

mule-deer-alpine.preferredHabitat: High summer meadows and shrubland with clean water
mule-deer-alpine.fact: Mule deer clear rocks and logs with a bouncy, four-footed hop.
mule-deer-alpine.role: A picky high-country plant eater. It spends summer in mountain meadows and shrubs, then walks downhill each fall. It picks the softest, richest leaves and buds. Cougars hunt it most, and eagles and coyotes take fawns.

fox-alpine.shelter: Dens dug in soil, often taken over from other animals
fox-alpine.preferredHabitat: High country with rocky cover and lots of small prey
fox-alpine.fact: Red foxes often move into holes dug by rabbits or marmots. They skip the digging.
fox-alpine.role: A mid-sized mountain hunter. It takes pikas, marmots, and ground birds, plus bugs and berries. It listens for prey moving under the snow, then dives in headfirst. Golden eagles are its main danger here.

pine-marten.diet: Voles, red squirrels, pikas, hares, birds, eggs, bugs, and berries
pine-marten.fact: Pine martens hunt under the winter snow, in tunnels others cannot reach.
pine-marten.role: A quick weasel of the treeline. It hunts voles, squirrels, pikas, and young hares. It adds berries and bugs in season. It roams over rough forest and rock, and even under the snow. Great horned owls, eagles, and bigger meat eaters hunt it.

clarks-nutcracker.preferredHabitat: High pine forest and treeline near pine seeds
clarks-nutcracker.fact: It can find thousands of buried seed stores months later, even under snow.
clarks-nutcracker.role: A mountain bird that gathers and buries thousands of pine seeds, so it plants the very forest it needs. Its buried food lets it raise chicks in deep winter. It also takes bugs and small animals when it can.

alpine-butterfly.diet: Young ones eat stonecrop. Adults drink from stonecrop and daisies
alpine-butterfly.shelter: No nest. Young hide in leaves and rocks. Eggs wait out the winter
alpine-butterfly.preferredHabitat: Rocky open high slopes where stonecrop grows
alpine-butterfly.fact: Its pale red and black wings warn hunters that it tastes bad.
alpine-butterfly.role: A tough mountain butterfly. Its caterpillars eat only stonecrop, and the adults drink from meadow flowers. Its bright wings warn that it tastes bad. Birds and spiders that ignore the warning still catch a few.

bumblebee-alpine.shelter: Group nests in holes in the ground and old mouse burrows
bumblebee-alpine.preferredHabitat: High flower meadows, often above the tree line
bumblebee-alpine.fact: This bee’s tongue got shorter between 1966 and 2014 as flowers grew scarce.
bumblebee-alpine.role: A cold-hardy bumblebee with a long tongue. It moves pollen for deep mountain flowers. It shivers its wing muscles to warm up and fly in near-freezing air. Its nests are underground. Birds, crab spiders, and robber flies catch the workers.

snowmelt-trout.diet: Bugs from the water and the land. Bigger ones also eat small fish
snowmelt-trout.shelter: Cold, clear pools and cut-away banks. Gravel shallows for eggs
snowmelt-trout.fact: Native cutthroat trout lose out to brown and brook trout brought in from elsewhere.
snowmelt-trout.role: A native cold-water fish. Where it lives, the mountain stream is clean and healthy. It picks bugs off the current, and big ones take smaller fish. Trout brought in from elsewhere crowd it out and eat it.

tidepool-crab.diet: Mostly algae, plus bits of waste, worms, snails, and dead animals
tidepool-crab.fact: Striped shore crabs eat algae. They also eat dead things, and even each other after they shed their shell.
tidepool-crab.role: A common shore crab. It scrapes algae off the rocks and cleans up dead animals. Gulls, shorebirds, and bigger crabs all eat it, so it moves food from the algae up to the hunters.

sea-turtle.diet: Mostly sea grass and algae as an adult. Eats more kinds when young
sea-turtle.preferredHabitat: Clean shallow water with sea grass and a quiet beach
sea-turtle.fact: Green sea turtles come back to nest on the same beach where they hatched decades before.
sea-turtle.role: The only sea turtle that eats mostly plants. Adults graze sea grass and algae, which keeps the beds healthy, and the young start out eating both plants and animals. When its eggs do well, the water is clean and the beaches are quiet.

american-goldfinch.diet: Almost all seeds: thistle, sunflower, aster, and grass
american-goldfinch.preferredHabitat: Weedy fields and open land with thistle, sunflower, and asters
american-goldfinch.fact: Goldfinches eat only plants. They nest late in summer so thistle fluff is ready to line the nest.
american-goldfinch.role: A seed eater that lives on thistle and other flower seeds. So it spreads those seeds across the meadow. It is small and common, so quick hawks and small owls catch it.

eastern-bluebird.diet: Mostly bugs off the ground: caterpillars, beetles, crickets. Fruit in winter
eastern-bluebird.shelter: A grass-lined nest in tree holes, old woodpecker holes, or boxes
eastern-bluebird.fact: An eastern bluebird can spot a tiny bug in the grass 60 feet away. Then it drops down and grabs it.
eastern-bluebird.role: A bug eater that nests in tree holes. It watches from a perch, then drops on caterpillars, beetles, and grasshoppers, and eats berries in winter. So it holds bugs down and spreads fruit seeds. It fights for nest holes, and hawks and small owls hunt it.

leafcutter-bee.diet: Adults eat nectar and pollen from many kinds of flowers
leafcutter-bee.preferredHabitat: Meadows and gardens with many flowers and holes to nest in
leafcutter-bee.fact: Female leafcutter bees cut neat circles from leaves to build and seal their nest.
leafcutter-bee.role: A bee that lives alone and moves pollen for many meadow and farm plants. It carries pollen on its belly. It lines its nest with cut leaves and packs each room with pollen and nectar for its young. Spiders and birds catch the adults.

painted-lady.diet: Adults drink from daisy-like flowers. Young eat thistle and mallow
painted-lady.shelter: Rests on plants. Young build silk nests on the plants they eat
painted-lady.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and rough ground with thistles and flowers
painted-lady.fact: Painted ladies travel thousands of miles across continents. They are one of the most widespread butterflies on Earth.
painted-lady.role: A butterfly that travels far. It drinks from many kinds of flowers and moves pollen as it goes. Its caterpillars eat thistle, mallow, and more than 100 other plants. When numbers boom, huge groups fly off together. Birds, wasps, and spiders eat both the adults and the young.

american-badger.diet: Digs out squirrels, gophers, voles, and mice. Also eats bugs
american-badger.shelter: Digs its own big burrows. A very strong digger
american-badger.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and grassland with soft soil and mice to hunt
american-badger.fact: Badgers sometimes team up with coyotes. The badger digs prey out below while the coyote catches the ones that run.
american-badger.role: A meat eater that digs prey right out of their tunnels. That keeps ground squirrel and vole numbers down. The holes it leaves behind help other animals. Almost nothing hunts a grown badger in this meadow.

pileated-woodpecker.diet: Carpenter ants and wood beetle grubs. Also termites, berries, and nuts
pileated-woodpecker.shelter: Cuts a new square nest hole each year in big dead trees
pileated-woodpecker.fact: Its deep square holes can be big enough to snap a small tree in half.
pileated-woodpecker.role: This big woodpecker builds homes for the whole forest. Its large holes become nests for wood ducks, flying squirrels, fishers, bats, and barred owls. It holds down carpenter ants and beetles. It opens up rotting wood so fungus and other tiny life can get in. Hawks and weasels eat it.

pacific-wren.diet: Beetles, caterpillars, ants, flies, and spiders. Some berries in winter
pacific-wren.preferredHabitat: Very old pine forest with thick undergrowth near streams
pacific-wren.fact: Pacific wren numbers rise near streams with salmon runs. The fish feed the bugs the wrens eat.
pacific-wren.role: The Pacific wren eats the small creatures of the shady forest floor. That food then feeds hawks, crows, and weasels. It needs damp old forest full of fallen logs, and streams fed by salmon. So it shows how healthy both the forest and the water are. It nests low in root tangles and rotting wood.

rough-skinned-newt.shelter: Under rotting logs, rocks, and leaves. In ponds when breeding
rough-skinned-newt.preferredHabitat: Coastal pine forest near still or slow water
rough-skinned-newt.fact: Its skin holds enough poison to kill several adults. Garter snakes have been in an arms race with it for ages.
rough-skinned-newt.role: The rough-skinned newt eats bugs, worms, and frog eggs, so it shapes what lives in a wetland. Its skin holds a very strong poison. Garter snakes have slowly become able to handle it. That back-and-forth is one of the best-known stories in biology. The poison keeps almost everything else from eating the newt.

northern-flying-squirrel.diet: Mostly fungus from underground. Also lichen, seeds, nuts, and bugs
northern-flying-squirrel.shelter: Tree holes, old woodpecker holes, and branch nests. Huddles in winter
northern-flying-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Old pine forest with a closed roof of leaves and lots of fungi
northern-flying-squirrel.fact: Fungus spores show up in almost every flying squirrel dropping. It is the forest’s key spreader of them.
northern-flying-squirrel.role: The northern flying squirrel spreads the underground fungus that pine and fir trees need to feed. That teamwork of squirrel, fungus, and tree is what lets the forest grow back. Owls, martens, and fishers eat the squirrel. So food moves from the fungus all the way up to the top hunters.

wood-duck.diet: Acorns, seeds, and water plants. Ducklings also eat bugs and snails
wood-duck.shelter: Only nests in tree holes and nest boxes near water
wood-duck.preferredHabitat: Low leafy woods and wooded swamps with slow water and hollow trees
wood-duck.fact: A day after hatching, wood duck ducklings jump from nest holes up to 50 feet high and land unhurt.
wood-duck.role: Wood ducks tie the flooded woods and the marsh together. They spread acorn and water-plant seeds and hold down the small life of the shallows. Great horned owls, mink, raccoons, and snapping turtles eat them. They nest in old woodpecker holes, so lots of wood ducks means the wooded wetland is healthy.

belted-kingfisher.diet: Small fish and crayfish, plus other water life
belted-kingfisher.fact: Kingfishers dive headfirst into the water with their eyes shut to grab fish.

snapping-turtle.diet: Fish, water plants, dead animals, and almost anything it can catch
snapping-turtle.fact: Almost nothing hunts a grown snapping turtle. They can live for many years.
snapping-turtle.role: A heavy turtle with a hard shell. It waits on the pond bottom and eats almost anything. Grown ones sit near the top of the marsh food web. They eat fish, ducklings, plants, and dead animals.

rosy-finch.diet: Tiny mountain plant seeds and bugs, often picked off the snow
rosy-finch.preferredHabitat: High ground above the trees: rock, scree, cliffs, and ice
rosy-finch.fact: It nests higher than almost any other song bird in North America.
rosy-finch.role: A high-mountain bird that hops over snow and rock, gathering seeds blown in by the wind and bugs chilled by the cold. It nests in cracks in the rock above treeline. Falcons and hawks are its main danger.

american-pipit.preferredHabitat: Open high meadows and bare ground during nesting season
american-pipit.fact: It feeds at the edge of snowbanks, picking up bugs chilled after drifting up from below.
american-pipit.role: A slim bird that walks across open mountain meadows, bobbing its tail as it hunts bugs. It picks up cold, slow bugs at the edge of snowbanks. Hawks and nest raiders are its main threats.

ermine.diet: Small mice, mostly voles. Also pikas, birds, eggs, and bugs
ermine.role: A small, fierce weasel that lives on voles and other mice, and also takes young pikas and ground-bird eggs. It is thin enough to slip right into their burrows. Foxes, martens, and hawks hunt it in turn.

mountain-bluebird.shelter: Old woodpecker holes, tree holes, and nest boxes
mountain-bluebird.fact: It cannot dig its own hole, so it reuses old woodpecker holes and nest boxes.
mountain-bluebird.role: A bright blue bird of open high meadows. It hovers and drops on bugs in the air and adds berries when it turns cold. It nests in tree holes, so it needs old woodpecker holes. Hawks and nest raiders hunt it.

purple-shore-crab.diet: Sea lettuce and other green algae, plus the odd dead animal
purple-shore-crab.fact: They scrape green algae off rocks and scuttle sideways under stones at low tide.
purple-shore-crab.role: A small crab that scrapes algae off shore rocks. Now and then it cleans up dead animals too. Gulls, anemones, and tidepool fish eat it, so it moves food from the algae up the web.

coopers-hawk.diet: Mostly small and mid-sized birds. Also chipmunks, mice, and squirrels
coopers-hawk.preferredHabitat: Wood edges and open land with scattered trees near meadows
coopers-hawk.fact: Cooper’s hawks race through thick cover to surprise small birds. It is risky, and many end up with healed chest breaks.
coopers-hawk.role: A hawk that hunts other birds along meadow edges and thickets. It flies low and turns fast, so it can pluck sparrows, finches, and bluebirds out of cover. It keeps small-bird numbers down, but bigger hawks can push it out.

western-screech-owl.shelter: Sleeps and nests in tree holes, old woodpecker holes, and boxes
western-screech-owl.preferredHabitat: Wooded edges and brushy spots next to open meadows
western-screech-owl.fact: This tiny owl will take prey bigger than itself, even a rabbit.
western-screech-owl.role: A small night hunter that waits, then drops on mice and bugs. It picks up grasshoppers and beetles and grabs voles and mice off the ground. At night it holds down both bugs and mice in the meadow.

barred-owl.diet: Small mammals, birds, frogs, lizards, fish, and bugs
barred-owl.shelter: Big tree holes in old forest. Also old hawk, crow, or squirrel nests
barred-owl.preferredHabitat: Old mixed or pine forest near water with big hollow trees
barred-owl.fact: Barred owls sometimes wade into shallow water to catch fish. That is unusual for a woodland owl.
barred-owl.role: The barred owl is a mid-level hunter. It holds down mice, voles, chipmunks, squirrels, and frogs. It sits above the small animals it eats and below the great horned owl, which is its main threat. It needs big trees with holes, so it shows whether a forest is old and healthy.

fisher.diet: Small and mid-sized mammals: porcupines, hares, squirrels. Also birds and fruit
fisher.shelter: Dens in hollow trees, logs, stumps, and ground burrows. Young go high up
fisher.preferredHabitat: Thick pine and mixed forest with a closed leaf roof and hollow trees
fisher.fact: The fisher is one of the few hunters that kills porcupines. It goes for the face until it can flip it over.
fisher.role: The fisher is a strong mid-level forest hunter. It is one of the few animals that can take a porcupine, which would otherwise damage lots of trees. It fills part of the gap left by big hunters that are gone. When fishers are around, the forest is old and well linked. Bobcats, foxes, and lynx eat the young ones.

prothonotary-warbler.shelter: Tree holes and nest boxes standing over water
prothonotary-warbler.fact: It is one of only two North American warblers that nest in tree holes.
prothonotary-warbler.role: A bright gold swamp bird. It picks bugs and spiders from over the water. Most warblers nest in the open. This one nests in tree holes, often right above the water.

pine-grosbeak.preferredHabitat: Open high spruce, fir, and pine forest near the tree line
pine-grosbeak.fact: A plump, unhurried finch of the cold high forests, nipping at buds and needles.
pine-grosbeak.role: A big, slow finch that lives almost only on pine buds, seeds, and fruit, adding bugs to feed its young. It helps spread tree and shrub seeds. Martens, small hawks, and foxes eat it, mostly at the nest.

praying-mantis.diet: Waits and grabs live bugs, like bees and grasshoppers
praying-mantis.preferredHabitat: Meadows and brushy edges with thick plants to hide in
praying-mantis.fact: A praying mantis can turn its head almost all the way around. No other insect can.
praying-mantis.role: A hunter that sits still and waits, then grabs prey with its spiky front legs faster than you can blink. It eats grasshoppers, bees, beetles, and other bugs, which helps keep bug numbers in check. Birds, garter snakes, and small owls eat it.

little-brown-bat.diet: Bugs only: midges, mayflies, moths, and mosquitoes
little-brown-bat.shelter: Sleeps in tree hollows, under bark, and in buildings. Winters in caves
little-brown-bat.preferredHabitat: Forest near streams, ponds, and clearings for catching bugs in the air
little-brown-bat.fact: A cold-loving fungus has killed more than 90% of little brown bats at many winter caves.
little-brown-bat.role: Little brown bats eat a huge number of bugs. One bat can eat half its own weight in a night, which holds down forest and water pests. They tie the bug layer to bigger hunters like owls, fishers, and snakes. A sickness called white-nose has killed most of them.

ensatina.diet: Small crawlers: worms, ants, beetles, spiders, centipedes, and snails
ensatina.shelter: Under rocks, bark, and logs on the forest floor. Goes underground when dry
ensatina.fact: Ensatinas have no lungs and breathe through their skin. They can drop a wriggling, poison-laced tail to escape.
ensatina.role: The ensatina is a common hunter of the forest floor. It holds down centipedes, millipedes, and sowbugs. That links the dead-leaf world to bigger animals. It has no lungs and breathes through its skin, so it needs damp, whole forest. That makes it a good sign of how wet the ground is. Garter snakes, raccoons, and jays eat it.

spotted-towhee.diet: Bugs and small crawlers in summer. Seeds, acorns, and berries in winter
spotted-towhee.preferredHabitat: Brushy forest edges and scrub with deep leaf litter
spotted-towhee.fact: The spotted towhee feeds with a two-footed backward hop that flicks leaves aside.
spotted-towhee.role: The spotted towhee feeds on the ground and ties the bug layer to the seed layer. It eats ground beetles and caterpillars in summer and spreads seeds in winter. It nests on the ground, so foxes, raccoons, and snakes get the nests while hawks and owls take the adults. Its scratching turns over the leaf litter.

spotted-turtle.diet: Water plants, bugs, worms, snails, and other small crawlers
spotted-turtle.fact: Each spotted turtle wears its own pattern of yellow dots on its shell.
spotted-turtle.role: A small turtle that is getting rare. It hunts plants and small water animals below the surface. It suns on logs and buries itself in mud when scared.

white-crowned-sparrow.diet: Mostly weed and grass seeds, plus caterpillars, beetles, and other bugs
white-crowned-sparrow.fact: Young white-crowns learn their song from the neighbours nearby.
white-crowned-sparrow.role: A sparrow that feeds on the ground at the edge of mountain meadows and low twisted trees. It eats seeds and summer bugs, spreads seeds, and feeds bug young to its chicks. Foxes, weasels, and martens take the adults and raid its low nests.

meadow-vole.fact: Voles mow narrow paths through the grass. They are tidy little roads they patrol between burrow doors.
meadow-vole.role: A tiny mouse that almost every hunter eats, and it has babies fast. It turns meadow plants into food for everyone else. Its eating and its little grass paths shape the grass layer. Hawks, owls, foxes, snakes, and badgers all count on it.

river-otter.fact: River otters can hold their breath for up to eight minutes while hunting.
river-otter.role: A quick swimmer that hunts fish and crayfish through the channels. Otters hold down fish and frog numbers. Seeing one means the water is clean and well linked.

muskrat.fact: Muskrats can stay under water for up to 15 minutes on one breath.
muskrat.role: A mostly plant-eating rodent that cuts reeds and cattails. That opens lanes of open water for ducks and other marsh life. Mink and otters eat it.

red-winged-blackbird.fact: Male red-winged blackbirds can hide their red shoulder patches. They flash them whenever they want.
red-winged-blackbird.role: A loud, common marsh bird that eats bugs and seeds. Males guard their reed patch hard. One patch may hold a dozen nests.

painted-turtle.fact: Painted turtles spend winter under the ice. They take in air through their skin.
painted-turtle.role: A turtle that suns itself, eats plants, and hunts bugs and small fish. It cleans up dead animals too. The young eat mostly meat and eat more plants as they grow.

chorus-frog.fact: A chorus frog’s call carries up to half a mile across the marsh.
chorus-frog.role: A tiny frog that eats small bugs. Its spring song fills the marsh. Herons, mink, and snakes all need it for food.

kit-fox.fact: The smallest wild dog in North America. Its huge ears hear prey and let out heat.
kit-fox.role: A small desert fox that hunts mice and rabbits at night. It hardly ever drinks, since it gets water from its food. Coyotes are its biggest danger.

coyote.fact: The noisiest wild mammal in North America. A howling pack sounds like far more animals.
coyote.role: The most flexible hunter in the desert. It eats mice, rabbits, fruit, and dead animals. It is the top mammal hunter here and the main killer of kit foxes. Its howls carry for miles at dusk.

kangaroo-rat.fact: Kangaroo rats never sweat or pant. They live on water made from the dry seeds they eat.
kangaroo-rat.role: A seed-eating desert rodent and key food animal. It buries seeds, which shapes which plants grow. Rattlesnakes, owls, and foxes all live on it.

jackrabbit.fact: A jackrabbit’s huge ears work like radiators. They let out body heat to keep it cool.

gambels-quail.fact: One male keeps watch from a perch while the rest of the group feeds below.
gambels-quail.role: A friendly ground bird that eats seeds, greens, and cactus fruit. Coyotes, bobcats, and desert hawks all need it for food. Flocks scratch through the brush together.

horned-lizard.fact: Texas horned lizards can squirt blood from their eyes to startle a hunter.
horned-lizard.role: A lizard that eats mostly one kind of ant and has a big belly to hold them. Roadrunners, hawks, shrikes, and snakes hunt it.

collared-lizard.fact: The collared lizard runs on its back legs like a tiny dinosaur, tail out behind.
collared-lizard.role: A quick hunter that waits among the rocks. Then it grabs bugs and smaller lizards. It hunts desert bugs and baby lizards.

tarantula.fact: A desert tarantula may live 25 years, most of it within a few feet of one burrow.
tarantula.role: A big spider that lives many years. At night it waits in its hole and grabs bugs and other small creatures. Birds, snakes, and wasps hunt it.

scorpion.fact: Scorpions glow blue-green under black light. Nobody is quite sure why.
scorpion.role: The biggest scorpion in North America. At night it waits and grabs bugs, spiders, and even other scorpions. Owls, snakes, and lizards eat it.

desert-bee.fact: Cactus bees nest alone, but thousands of them share the same patch of ground.
desert-bee.role: A bee that lives alone. It moves pollen for desert cactus like prickly pear and cholla. It eats nectar and pollen, and the cactus needs it to make fruit.

sea-star.fact: The classic key animal. Take it away and mussels take over the whole shore.
sea-star.role: The best-known key animal of the rocky shore. By eating mussels it sets how far down the mussel bed can grow. That leaves room for many other kinds of life.

anemone.fact: Its green glow comes from algae living inside it. The algae share the sugars they make.
anemone.role: A tidepool hunter that waits and grabs whatever the waves knock loose. It also grows tiny algae inside itself for extra food. It is a small hunter that helps clean up loose shellfish and crabs.

mussel.fact: One mussel cleans several liters of sea water an hour as it feeds.
mussel.role: A filter feeder that builds reefs. Its beds make homes for countless small animals. It is the key food that ties the top shore hunters together, from sea stars to sea otters to oystercatchers.

clam.fact: You can guess a clam’s age by counting the rings on its shell.
clam.role: A shellfish buried in the sand. It strains its food from the water, which helps keep the sea clean. Sea otters, shorebirds, crabs, and gulls dig it up or crack it open.

shorebird.fact: Snowy plover chicks can run and feed themselves within hours of hatching.
shorebird.role: A small beach bird that snaps up tiny sea bugs and kelp flies along the tide line. It is at risk and needs quiet beaches. Its nests fail easily where beaches are busy.

pelican.fact: Brown pelicans dive from up to 65 feet, twisting to protect the neck as they hit.
pelican.role: A fish hunter that dives from the air. It nearly died out from the pesticide DDT and then came back, which is one of the great wins for wildlife. Where pelicans are, the water holds healthy schools of small fish.

cormorant.fact: Cormorant feathers soak up water on purpose. Less float means better diving.
cormorant.role: A bird that dives and chases fish over reefs and open water. It needs clear water and lots of fish, so lots of cormorants means the rocky shore is doing well.

harbor-seal.fact: Harbor seals can sleep under water. They come up to breathe without fully waking.
harbor-seal.role: A sea hunter that eats whatever fish is easy to catch. Sharks and killer whales hunt it out at sea, but on this healed coast it sits near the top of the food web.

american-bittern.fact: The bittern freezes with its bill up and sways like a reed to vanish in the marsh.
american-bittern.role: A shy hunter of the reeds. It stands perfectly still, then grabs fish, frogs, and bugs. Its stripes let it hide in plain sight.

marsh-wren.fact: Males build many spare nests and even break their neighbours’ eggs.
marsh-wren.role: A tiny, feisty bug eater of the reeds. It picks bugs and spiders off the stems, and males build several fake nests to win a mate.

gila-woodpecker.fact: The holes it leaves in cactus later shelter elf owls, tiny owls, and kestrels.
gila-woodpecker.role: A woodpecker that nests in cactus and builds homes for the whole desert. It eats bugs, cactus fruit, and berries. Its old holes shelter many other animals. Hawks, snakes, and bobcats hunt it.

cactus-wren.fact: Cactus wrens use their ball-shaped nests all year, even for sleeping.
cactus-wren.role: The biggest wren in North America. It picks spiders and bugs off the brush and eats cactus fruit. It gets most of its water from its food. Snakes, roadrunners, and hawks take it and raid its nests.

desert-iguana.fact: The desert iguana stays busy in heat that sends other lizards into the shade.
desert-iguana.role: A heat-loving lizard that eats mostly creosote bush flowers and leaves. It is a plant eater and food for snakes, hawks, and foxes. It waits out the hottest hours in a burrow.

kangaroo-mouse.fact: It lives on water made from its food. It may never drink in its whole life.

banded-gecko.fact: Unlike most geckos, this one has eyelids that move, and it squeaks when caught.
banded-gecko.role: A small night gecko that hunts bugs, spiders, and even baby scorpions. It is food for bigger lizards, snakes, and roadrunners. It can drop its tail to get away.

sanderling.fact: Sanderlings chase the waves back out in busy little sprints to grab stranded creatures.
sanderling.role: A small sandpiper that chases the waves in and out, eating tiny sea bugs and worms the surf digs up. Falcons hunt it. Its winter flocks show how healthy open sandy beaches are.

black-oystercatcher.fact: Its long red bill pries shellfish open and cuts the muscle before the shell can shut.
black-oystercatcher.role: A shore bird that pries mussels and limpets off the rock. It feeds when the tide lets it. It only does well where there is plenty of shellfish, so it shows how healthy the shore is.

brant-goose.fact: Whole flocks of brant depend on eelgrass beds to fuel their long trips.
brant-goose.role: A small sea goose. It eats almost nothing but eelgrass and green algae in shallow bays. Since it needs eelgrass, healthy brant flocks mean the sea grass beds are whole.

snowy-plover.fact: Western snowy plovers nest in tiny scrapes right on the open sand.
snowy-plover.role: A beach-nesting bird that is at risk. It eats tiny animals along the sand and tide line. It is easily scared off its nest, so it only does well on quiet, protected dune beaches.

costas-hummingbird.fact: A male dives past a female with a high whistle. His purple throat flashes in the sun.
costas-hummingbird.role: A small desert hummingbird that drinks nectar from agave, chuparosa, and other blooms and eats tiny bugs. It moves lots of pollen. Snakes and hunting birds catch it.

acorn-woodpecker.fact: It drills thousands of holes in one tree and stores a single acorn in each.
acorn-woodpecker.role: A woodpecker that lives in groups and stuffs acorns into shared storage trees. It also catches flying bugs. Its acorn stashes and its old holes help other animals, so it is a key builder in oak woods.

common-yellowthroat.fact: The male’s black mask is a signal that rivals will attack on sight.

phainopepla.fact: This bird spreads desert mistletoe seeds. The two depend on each other.
phainopepla.role: A shiny black desert bird that lives mostly on mistletoe berries in winter and catches bugs in the air. It is the main spreader of mistletoe seeds. Snakes and hawks hunt it.

antelope-squirrel.fact: It carries its tail arched over its back like a parasol for shade.

annas-hummingbird.role: A hummingbird that stays on the coast all year. It drinks nectar and eats small bugs. As it feeds it moves pollen for shrubs like manzanita and gooseberry. It links coastal flowers to the wider food web.

mink.role: A bold hunter that swims after fish, frogs, and even muskrats. Mink are mid-sized hunters that help hold down small marsh animals.

mallard-duck.role: A duck that tips head down to eat seeds, plants, and small water bugs. Its ducklings and eggs feed many marsh hunters.

sandhill-crane.role: A tall bird of the open marsh. It digs for roots and grain and snaps up bugs and small animals. When cranes are here, the wetland is wide and healthy.

hooded-merganser.role: A small diving duck. Its bill has saw-like teeth for holding slippery prey. It chases fish, crayfish, and bugs under water. It nests in tree holes.

roadrunner.role: A bird that runs down lizards, bugs, scorpions, and snakes on foot. It is a key hunter of small desert reptiles and bugs. Coyotes and hawks hunt it.

desert-tortoise.role: A plant eater that lives a very long time and builds homes for others. Its holes can run more than 10 metres and shelter snakes, lizards, mice, and bugs. Grown tortoises have thick shells, so few things can hurt them.

rattlesnake.role: A snake with venom that waits, then strikes. It is a big check on desert mouse numbers. It swallows prey whole and only needs to eat every few weeks. Roadrunners, hawks, and other snakes hunt it.

hermit-crab.role: A tidepool cleaner. It eats algae and dead animals. It moves into empty snail shells to stay safe. Gulls, fish, and octopus all eat it.

gull.role: A bold bird that eats almost anything. It cleans up dead animals and hunts crabs, shellfish, and even sea stars, which links many kinds of prey to the top of the food web. Foxes and coyotes take gulls and their eggs on land.

unlock.label: Bring Willow Meadow to 60% health. Welcome 10 meadow animals. Craft a Forest Restoration Kit.

forest.restorationGoal: Grow back the low plants, raise nesting trees and dead wood, and welcome the forest animals home.

unlock.label: Bring Old Hollow Forest to 80% health with 10 forest animals back. Welcome 25 animals in all. Craft a Wetland Restoration Kit.

wetland.restorationGoal: Bring back shallow water, reed beds, and mud banks so wetland life can return.

unlock.label: Bring Rushwater Wetland to 80% health with 13 wetland animals back. Welcome 45 animals in all. Craft a Scrubland Restoration Kit.

desert.description: A desert flat eaten down to bare ground. With no brush and no burrows, the heat keeps everything away.
desert.restorationGoal: Plant cactus and brush, build shade and burrows, and bring the desert back to life.

unlock.label: Bring Redstone Scrubland to 80% health with 15 desert animals back. Welcome 65 animals in all. Craft an Alpine Restoration Kit.

alpine.restorationGoal: Bring back mountain grass and snowmelt pools. Add rocky shelter for the animals up high.

unlock.label: Bring Graywind Heights to 80% health with 17 alpine animals back. Welcome 85 animals in all. Craft a Migration Path Marker.

coastal.description: A worn stretch of coast where the open sea breaks on the east edge. The dunes washed out and the tidepools are empty. Sea glass, kelp, coral, and the odd pearl still wash up.
coastal.restorationGoal: Hold the dunes in place, bring back tidepools and kelp, and open the shore to coast life again.

meadow.description: A meadow beside your home that used to bloom. Now it is dusty and quiet. The native grasses were stripped out, and the bugs that fed on them left too.
meadow.restorationGoal: Plant grass and wild flowers. Add water and shelter. Help 10 meadow animals come back.

welcome-grasshopper.flavor: You did it. You gathered, built, shaped the land, and welcomed your first neighbor. One hop in the grass, and you already know how to bring back a whole meadow.
welcome-grasshopper.hint: Every caretaker starts with one small arrival.

forager.hint: Gather, and keep gathering. Build a real pile.

makers-hands.hint: Keep crafting. One item will not heal a meadow.

green-thumb.flavor: Ten living things in soil you got ready yourself. Half of this work is just patience with a watering can.

meadow-first-bloom.hint: Grow the meadow well past its first lonely guest.

meadow-pollinators.flavor: Monarch, bumblebee, leafcutter, lady beetle, painted lady. They work for free. They turn flowers into seeds, and seeds into more meadow.

meadow-apex.flavor: A fox only stays where there are voles and rabbits to hunt. So when it shows up, everything below it is finally fed.

meadow-reborn.flavor: Every animal that belongs here is home. The meadow does not need you to hum anymore. But it remembers who started it.

forest-understory.flavor: Ferns, shrubs, a squirrel arguing with a woodpecker, newts under the dead wood. A forest is built from the ground up, not the top down.

forest-reborn.flavor: From a cut-over hush to a full forest. Three layers, and every wing in between.

wetland-first-water.flavor: Shape the water and the water brings its own crowd. Frogs, water striders, dragonflies skating the top, a heron in the shallows.

wetland-engineer.hint: Welcome the one who builds homes for everyone else.

wetland-lakemaker.flavor: Enough open water to hold a sky. Turtles sun themselves, ducks dive, and the marsh has a center again.
wetland-lakemaker.hint: Open enough water, all in one piece, to hold a sky.

wetland-restored.flavor: Reeds where there was cracked mud. Channels that really flow. A wetland cleans all the water that leaves it, and asks for nothing.

desert-burrows.flavor: In the desert, the good spots are underground. A tortoise digs a burrow and an owl takes the spare room. Nobody wastes a hole here.

desert-hunter.flavor: A hunter that can wait out the heat means there is finally enough prey to wait for.

desert-reborn.flavor: The hardest land here, fully alive. From the elf owl in the cactus to the tarantula under the stone.

alpine-haypile.flavor: The pika spends all summer stacking little hay piles for a winter it refuses to sleep through. Tiny animal, huge work ethic.
alpine-haypile.hint: Welcome back the little hay stacker of the rocks.

alpine-reborn.flavor: Goat to ptarmigan to trout in the snowmelt. The whole high country, brought back against the wind.

coastal-keystone.flavor: The classic key animal. Take the sea star away and mussels take everything. Put it back and the whole tidepool shares the rock again.
coastal-keystone.hint: Bring back the one animal that holds the tidepool together.

coastal-otter.flavor: Otters eat the urchins that eat the kelp. So an otter on the water means a forest under it. Few animals do more with a full belly.

coastal-reborn.flavor: From whale spouts to clams. The last and wildest stretch of the preserve, complete.

well-stocked.flavor: A thousand fallen things gathered. You stopped scraping by long ago. This is a real store.

master-builder.hint: Place homes until the whole preserve shows your hand.

master-gardener.flavor: Seventy-five living things put in the ground, one sprout at a time. This work is mostly just showing up with a watering can.

landscaper.hint: Shape soil and water across the preserve, over and over.

fully-equipped.hint: Take your basket, shovel, and watering can to the top.

naturalist.flavor: Every guide filled in. Every animal known. You do not just host wildlife now. You understand it.

recipe-collector.flavor: Seventy-five different things, each built at least once. You have used almost every tool on the bench.
recipe-collector.hint: Build a little of almost everything on the bench.

full-house.flavor: A hundred kinds of neighbor. The preserve is not healing anymore. It is thriving.

field-notes.hint: Watch your wild neighbors, again and again, all over.

three-restored.flavor: Three broken places, brought most of the way home. The preserve is tipping from healing to healed.

caretaker-of-the-whole.flavor: Every animal in every area is home. The broken land you found is now, simply, wild. The rarest star there is.

wildflower-patch.description: Mixed native wildflowers. Bees can spot it from far away.

sunflower-patch.description: Tall sunflowers that feed seed-eating birds all season.

willow-tree.description: The tree this place is named for, grown from a watered bed.

butterfly-flowers.description: Milkweed and nectar flowers, planted just for butterflies.

pollinator-garden.description: A thick, all-season feast for bees and butterflies.

small-pond.description: A clay-lined pond. Clean drinking water changes everything.

fern-spring.description: A mossy wet spot ringed with ferns. Damp ground wakes up the whole forest floor.

rock-pile.description: Sun-warm stones with cool gaps below. Bugs, lizards, and pikas love it.

wooden-bridge.description: A strong plank bridge. Put it on open water to cross rivers and lakes.

nesting-tree.description: A fast-growing native tree for squirrels, owls, and nuthatches.

standing-deadwood.description: A dead tree held up safely. Prime woodpecker property.

reed-bed.description: Thick replanted reeds. A nursery for frogs, dragonflies, and blackbirds.

mud-bank.description: A soft shaped bank for digging and sunning. Needs the restoration shovel.

cattail-stand.description: Tall cattails at the water edge. Cover for marsh birds and shade for the shallows.

marsh-log.description: A half-sunk log. Turtles and frogs sun on it and otters slip under it.

lily-pool.description: Still, clean water covered in lily pads. Dragonflies and frogs raise their young here.

burrow-mound.description: A starter bank for diggers. Needs the restoration shovel.

kelp-wrack.description: A safe line of washed-up kelp. A feast for the whole beach.

coastal-nesting-area.description: A roped-off quiet strip of upper beach for nesting.

coral-garden.description: Moved coral pieces that grow back into a living reef. Food and shelter for the whole shore.

sea-glass-lantern.description: Beach glass set in driftwood. It throws soft sea-green light at dusk.

pearl-display.description: A polished shell stand showing the rarest pearls the shore gives up.

sea-glass-path.description: Smooth sea glass pressed into the sand. A shiny path that keeps boots off the dunes.

small-chest.description: A woven and wood chest. Holds 120 materials. Anything in here can be used for crafting from anywhere.

field-journal-stand.description: A little stand for your journal. Read it wherever you put one.

wetland-restoration-kit.description: Liners, filters, and channel tools. Everything you need to bring water back. Making it helps open Rushwater Wetland.

forest-restoration-kit.description: Seed mixes, twine, and trail tools to open the grown-over forest path. Making it helps open Old Hollow Forest.

scrubland-restoration-kit.description: Sleds and tough cuttings to carry this work into the dry scrubland. Making it helps open Redstone Scrubland.

garden-arch.description: A flowery arch that frames a path and feeds passing bees.

trail-signpost.description: A hand-painted sign to guide visitors through the preserve.

gazebo.description: An open shelter with a roof. A pretty centerpiece and a shady place to watch from.

clover-patch.description: Low clover and trefoil. Nectar for bees and food for rabbits.

fern-grove.description: Shady arching ferns that carpet the forest floor.

alder-snag.description: A dead alder left standing. A perch and a nest hole above the water.

agave-rosette.description: A spiky plant whose tall flower feeds desert bees.

ocotillo.description: Whip-like stalks with red tips. Cover and nectar in the open flats.

heather-mat.description: A low mountain mat of heather flowers above the rocks.

eelgrass-bed.description: Waving eelgrass. A nursery for fish and food for sea geese.

oyster-bed.description: A clump of shellfish that cleans the tide and feeds shore birds.

daisy-patch.description: Bright white daisies that open with the morning sun.

bulrush.description: Tall bulrushes with brown velvet heads along the bank.

gentian-patch.description: Bright blue mountain gentians, kept low by the wind.

nectar-feeder.description: A sweet agave feeder that draws hummingbirds and nectar bats.

shore-pine.description: A salt-bent pine that holds the back dunes and shelters shore birds.

bald-cypress.description: A tall swamp cypress with feathery needles and a wide, knobby base.

desert-ironwood.description: A dense, slow-growing tree. It shelters young plants in the open desert.

quaking-aspen.description: White-barked aspen whose golden leaves shake in the mountain wind.

birdhouse.description: A hand-built birdhouse on a post. Charming, even when empty.

flower-cart.description: A little wooden cart spilling over with cut flowers.

hammock.description: A woven hammock hung between two posts for lazy afternoons.

flower-pots.description: A neat row of clay pots full of blooms.

insect-hotel.description: A stack of hollow stems and bark where bees and beetles nest.

duck-nest-box.description: A raised wooden box where water birds raise their young.

rock-crevice.description: Stacked slabs with shady cracks where lizards hide from the heat.

dew-basin.description: A shallow clay bowl that catches dew and rain. Precious desert water.

talus-pile.description: A jumble of broken rock. The tunnels and runways pikas love.

nesting-bluff.description: A built-up sandy bank with ledges for cliff-nesting sea birds.

pika-haypile.description: A pile of dried grass and flowers, cured the way pikas store hay for winter.

lichen-boulder.description: A weathered boulder crusted with lichen. Slow mountain grazing and a foothold for new life.

scree-slope.description: A shifting slope of broken rock, laced with the runways and hideouts of the high country.

snowbank-roost.description: A packed drift of late snow. A cool resting spot and a trickle of meltwater for hares and birds.

whitebark-cache.description: A hidden store of pine nuts. The seed bank nutcrackers and grosbeaks live on.

juniper-thicket.description: A low, tough juniper heavy with frosted berries. Cover and winter food where little else grows.

cliff-nest-niche.description: A sheltered gap in the cliff, mossy and tucked away for high country nesters.

crystal-spring.description: An ice-cold spring rising through quartz. The purest, coldest water up here.

summit-prayer-flags.description: A bright line of worn flags strung between stone piles, snapping in the wind.

obsidian-totem.description: A polished column of volcanic glass that catches the high light like dark, still water.

large-chest.description: A big iron-banded chest. Holds 500 materials. Your main store.

home-bed.description: A comfy bed for resting between days of work.

home-armchair.description: A soft armchair to sink into after a long day.

home-lamp.description: A soft floor lamp for cozy evenings inside.

rain-basin.description: A carved stone bowl that catches rain. A drinking spot for visiting animals.

sunstone-cairn.description: A stack of sun-baked stones that hold the day heat into the evening.

frostflower-planter.description: A planter of pale ice-blooms that keep their shape long after the snow goes.

frostflower-vase.description: A glass vase of ice-blooms for the windowsill. They never wilt.

stormglass-chandelier.description: A hanging cluster of lightning-glass shards that spreads cool light across the room.

boardwalk.description: A raised plank path. Cross the marsh without stepping on the reeds and mud.

heron-rookery.description: A tall marsh snag with a stick nest on top. Just the high, safe perch herons and egrets need.

dragonfly-pond.description: A clear pool ringed with reeds. Open water where dragonflies hunt and frogs and newts breed.

hiking-boots.description: Strong boots made from tough bark, springy moss, and woven reeds. Once made they are yours for good. Wear them to move a little faster.

basket.description: For gently picking up light things that grow back: seeds, berries, flowers, fiber, shells.

shovel.description: For carefully digging stones, clay, and sand, and getting ground ready.

2.effect: Shape mud banks and burrow mounds. Dig up 2 things at a time.
